Neonatal European bison calves exhibit a pronounced sexual dimorphism in body mass from the moment of birth. Female newborns typically weigh 24.4 kilograms [Wwb = 24.4 kilograms], a value that reflects the high maternal investment characteristic of this large-bodied bovid. In contrast, male neonates are noticeably heavier at birth, with a recorded mass of 27.6 kilograms [Wwb = 27.6 kilograms]. This difference in initial mass sets the stage for divergent growth trajectories between the sexes, a pattern commonly observed in polygynous ungulates where males must attain a larger body size to compete successfully for access to mates. The parturition event itself is preceded by a well-defined gestation period that, under the typical core body temperature of a healthy adult female, which is maintained at 38.4 °C [T = 38.4 °C], lasts for 270 days [tg = 270 days]. This length of gestation is consistent with the species' phylogenetic position among the Bovini and aligns with the substantial fetal growth required to produce a precocial calf capable of standing and following its mother shortly after birth. Furthermore, the considerable investment in each calf, which is born after a lengthy 270-day gestation, necessitates an extended period of maternal care that begins immediately following the birth of these 24.4- to 27.6-kilogram neonates.

As the calf matures and transitions from a milk-based diet to solid forage, the period of weaning represents a critical nutritional and behavioral milestone. Under standard physiological conditions at a core temperature of 38.4 °C [T = 38.4 °C], this transition typically occurs at 213 days since birth [tx = 213 days since birth]. At this juncture, the young animal has developed a functional rumen and begins to rely increasingly on grazing, though it may continue to nurse sporadically for a short time thereafter. The weaning process is gradual in this species, reflecting the complex social dynamics of the herd and the need for the juvenile to acquire sufficient gut microflora to digest fibrous plant matter. This period of nutritional independence at approximately seven months of age is a prerequisite for the subsequent phases of growth and, eventually, sexual maturation, which in European bison occurs at a considerably later age relative to the short weaning interval. The timing of weaning is influenced by maternal condition and resource availability in the environment.

Sexual maturation in European bison is a protracted process, with both sexes exhibiting a remarkably similar timeline for the onset of reproductive capability. Under the stable thermal environment of a 38.4 °C [T = 38.4 °C] core body temperature, females first attain puberty at 730 days since birth [tp = 730 days since birth], marking the age at which the first ovulation and oestrous cycle are theoretically possible, although successful breeding in free-ranging populations is often delayed by social hierarchy and nutritional constraints. Likewise, male calves reach puberty at 730 days since birth [tp = 730 days since birth], at which point testicular descent is complete and spermatogenesis has commenced at a temperature of 38.4 °C [T = 38.4 °C]. The synchrony in the timing of puberty between the sexes is notable, though it does not necessarily imply coincident reproductive activity, as young males may be excluded from mating by older, more dominant bulls for several additional years. This developmental schedule places the onset of adolescence at roughly two years of age, a value that situates the species within the typical range for slow-maturing, large herbivores. The coordinated timing likely reflects an evolutionary history wherein both sexes developed reproductive capacity at a similar age to maximize reproductive success in a social structure that requires substantial body size for competition.

The life history of the European bison is characterized by a slow pace of life, which is further underscored by its maximum reproductive rate and its considerable potential longevity. Under standard physiological conditions at a core body temperature of 38.4 °C [T = 38.4 °C], the maximum recorded reproductive output for a female is one calf per parturition event [N_R_i = one calf per parturition event], with a single calf being the norm per birth. This effectively yields a reproductive frequency of one event per year [F_R_i = one event per year], reflecting the long gestation and extended period of maternal care required by the precocial young. At the other end of the life cycle, the species is notable for its long lifespan; the maximum recorded longevity is approximately 26.4 years [am = approximately 26.4 years] at a temperature of 38.4 °C [T = 38.4 °C]. This extended period of life, exceeding a quarter of a century in the wild, allows for multiple reproductive attempts and a prolonged period of social learning. The combination of very low annual reproductive output and extended lifespan is typical of a K-selected life-history strategy among large terrestrial mammals.

The dramatic divergence in adult body mass between the sexes represents one of the most striking features of the European bison's life history. Females, having completed their somatic growth, attain an ultimate wet weight of 424 kilograms [Wwi = 424 kilograms], a mass that allows them to effectively forage and reproduce while remaining agile enough to navigate forested habitats. Males, in stark contrast, undergo a prolonged and intense period of post-pubertal growth that results in an adult mass of 634 kilograms [Wwi = 634 kilograms]. This substantial increase in male body size, representing a roughly 50 percent mass advantage over females, is a classic example of sexual selection driven by male-male competition for reproductive access. The energetic demands of achieving and maintaining this larger frame are considerable, and are likely a contributing factor to the higher mortality rates observed among adult males, which may prevent them from regularly realizing the species' full potential lifespan despite their impressive physical stature. This sexual size dimorphism places the European bison among the most dimorphic of the Bovini species.
